regions.name: Armenia
regions.summary: Home of the oldest winery ever found: a 6,100-year-old cave at Areni. High-altitude vineyards, volcanic soils and native grapes make fresh, mineral wines.
regions.climate: Continental with hot summers and cold winters; vineyards sit at 800 to 2,000 m, among the highest in the world.
regions.styles: Dry and fortified wines, especially from Areni (a light, spicy red) and Voskehat (a rich, floral white).
regions.classification: Wine regions: Ararat Valley, Vayots Dzor, Aragatsotn, Armavir, Tavush, Syunik, Kotayk and Shirak, with a growing system of appellations.
regions.history: In 2007 archaeologists found a 6,100-year-old winery in the Areni-1 cave, with a wine press, fermentation vats and storage jars. Armenian legend says Noah planted the first vineyard on the slopes of Mount Ararat.
facts: Areni-1 is the oldest known winery in the world.
Armenia's high elevations and sandy volcanic soils protected many vines from phylloxera, so lots of old, ungrafted vines survive.

regions.name: Ararat Valley
regions.summary: The wide plain around Yerevan, below Mount Ararat: the big source of Armenian brandy grapes and fortified wines, with hot summers.
regions.climate: Hot and dry in summer, cold in winter.

regions.name: Vayots Dzor
regions.summary: The 'Valley of Sorrow': a high, dry canyon landscape with the Areni cave and the home of the Areni grape. Vineyards climb to 1,700 m.

regions.name: Aragatsotn
regions.summary: The foothills of Mount Aragats, the highest peak in Armenia, with volcanic soils and old vineyards in the villages of Ashtarak and Karmrashen.

regions.name: Kotayk & Gegharkunik
regions.summary: Mountain slopes north-east of Yerevan and the shores of Lake Sevan: small, cool plots.

regions.name: Tavush
regions.summary: The forested north-east, on the border with Georgia: a cooler region with a long tradition of home winemaking.

regions.name: Syunik
regions.summary: The mountainous south, near the Iranian border, with a few high-altitude vineyards and ancient vines.

regions.name: Lori & Shirak
regions.summary: The high north-west plateau, too cold for most vines but with a few hardy plots.

regions.name: Southern Brazil
regions.summary: Brazil makes wine mostly in the south: sparkling wine and Merlot from the Italian-settled Serra Gaúcha, fresh reds and whites from the cooler heights of Santa Catarina and a rising Campanha. (There is also tropical winemaking in the São Francisco Valley in the north-east, with two harvests a year.)
regions.climate: Subtropical and humid, with heavy rain in summer. The vines sit on hills at 600 to 1,400 m to find cooler air.
regions.styles: Traditional-method and Moscato sparkling wine (Brazil's best), Merlot and Cabernet Franc, and ever finer still wines.
regions.classification: Indicações Geográficas (IGs) and Denominações de Origem: Vale dos Vinhedos (the first, 2002), Pinto Bandeira, Altos Montes, Farroupilha, Campanha Gaúcha and Campos de Cima da Serra.
regions.history: Italian immigrants arrived in the Serra Gaúcha in 1875 with vines and winemaking skills; they made wine from the hybrid Isabel grape for a century before European grapes took over.
facts: The Vale dos Vinhedos was Brazil's first geographical indication for wine, in 2002.
Brazil is among the world's top three sparkling-wine consumers per head in South America.

regions.name: Serra Gaúcha
regions.summary: The high hills in the north-east of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil's wine heartland: about 85% of national production, from Bento Gonçalves, Garibaldi and Caxias do Sul.

regions.name: Vale dos Vinhedos
regions.summary: The 'Valley of the Vineyards': Brazil's best-known wine landscape and its first official appellation (2002), with Merlot and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Pinto Bandeira
regions.summary: A higher, cooler area above Bento Gonçalves that is the heart of Brazil's top traditional-method sparkling wine.

regions.name: Campos de Cima da Serra
regions.summary: A high, cool plateau at over 1,000 m on the border of Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina.

regions.name: Campanha Gaúcha
regions.summary: The border area with Uruguay: low rolling pampas, sunny and dry, now producing about a third of the finer wines of Brazil.

regions.name: Serra do Sudeste
regions.summary: Granite hills at around 400 m in the south-east, a new, small area for elegant reds.

regions.name: Santa Catarina Highlands
regions.summary: São Joaquim and Urubici: vineyards at 900 to 1,400 m, among the highest in Brazil, with winters cold enough for snow.

regions.name: Bulgaria
regions.summary: An old wine land of the Thracians, with a Soviet-era export boom and a revival of native grapes: Mavrud, Melnik, Gamza and Rubin, plus excellent international varieties.
regions.climate: Continental in the north and Mediterranean in the south, with the Balkan Mountains between.
regions.styles: Rich, dark reds (Mavrud, Melnik), simple fresh whites and aromatic Misket.
regions.classification: Five wine regions (Danube Plain, Black Sea, Thracian Valley, Rose Valley, Struma Valley) with PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) appellations.
regions.history: The Thracians drank wine from the 2nd millennium BC, and Orpheus is said to have come from here. Bulgaria was the world's second-biggest wine exporter in the 1980s.
facts: Melnik is a tiny town in the south-west, famed for its sandstone pyramids and wine cellars cut into the rock.
Mavrud is among the oldest Bulgarian grapes, linked to a Thracian legend of a young man's dark wine.

regions.name: Danube Plain
regions.summary: The northern plain along the river Danube: Bulgaria's biggest area, with Gamza and Merlot in Vidin and Pleven.

regions.name: Black Sea
regions.summary: The eastern coast: cool breezes for fresh, light whites, with Dimiat and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Thracian Valley
regions.summary: The warm southern plain: Bulgaria's best-known red area, with Mavrud around Asenovgrad.

regions.name: Struma Valley
regions.summary: The far south-west near Greece and North Macedonia: the hottest, driest part, home of the Melnik grape, a dark, spicy red that ages well.

regions.name: Ontario, Quebec & Nova Scotia
regions.summary: Canada's cool-climate East. Ontario is the world's largest ice wine producer and a rising star for Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; Nova Scotia and Quebec grow crisp sparkling wines and hardy hybrids.
regions.climate: Cold continental winters. The Great Lakes (and the Atlantic in Nova Scotia) keep winter lows just above the point where vines die.
regions.styles: Ice wine (Vidal and Riesling), sparkling wine, Riesling, Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc.
regions.classification: Vintners Quality Alliance (VQA) designated viticultural areas: Niagara Peninsula, Prince Edward County, Lake Erie North Shore, Nova Scotia.
facts: Ice wine grapes are picked frozen by hand at -8°C or lower, often at night.
Prince Edward County sits on the same limestone as parts of Burgundy; growers there bury their vines each winter to protect them from the cold.

regions.name: Niagara Peninsula
regions.summary: Ontario's powerhouse, between lakes Ontario and Erie, with the Niagara Escarpment sheltering the vines. Excellent Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc and ice wine.

regions.name: Niagara-on-the-Lake
regions.summary: Flat, warm land near Lake Ontario; Niagara's biggest wineries and the world capital of ice wine.

regions.name: Beamsville & Twenty Mile Benches
regions.summary: Terraces below the Escarpment where cool breezes slow ripening, ideal for Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Prince Edward County
regions.summary: An island-like peninsula in Lake Ontario with thin limestone soil. It makes some of Canada's most Burgundian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Lake Erie North Shore
regions.summary: Ontario's warmest wine area, at the same latitude as northern California. It includes Pelee Island, Canada's most southerly vineyard.

regions.name: Annapolis Valley
regions.summary: A sheltered valley in Nova Scotia, with the Bay of Fundy's huge tides. Canada's best sparkling wines from the cold-climate grape L'Acadie Blanc.

regions.name: Eastern Townships
regions.summary: South-east Quebec near the Vermont border, where vines are buried or covered each winter and cold-hardy hybrids are made into whites, ice cider and fortified wine.

regions.name: British Columbia
regions.summary: Canada's biggest wine province: sunny, desert-like valleys in the interior and cool coastal islands, with fresh whites, Pinot Noir and serious Bordeaux-style reds.
regions.climate: The interior valleys are hot and dry, sheltered from the Pacific by mountains; the coast is cool and wet.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir, Merlot, Chardonnay, Riesling and ice wine; fresh aromatic whites and big, ripe reds in the south.
regions.classification: Geographical Indications (GIs) under the Vintners Quality Alliance (VQA): Okanagan Valley, Similkameen Valley, Fraser Valley, Vancouver Island and Gulf Islands.
facts: The Okanagan Valley is home to Canada's only true desert, at Osoyoos, where vines grow beside cactus.
More than 80% of Canadian ice wine is made in Ontario, but BC also makes it in cold years.

regions.name: Okanagan Valley
regions.summary: A 250 km valley of lakes from Vernon down to the US border: Canada's best-known and biggest wine region, with more than 80% of BC's vines.
regions.climate: Hot, dry summers (up to 40°C) and cool nights in the south; cooler in the north.

regions.name: Osoyoos & Oliver
regions.summary: The 'Golden Mile' and the desert far south: the hottest part of Canada, famous for ripe Merlot, Syrah and Bordeaux blends.

regions.name: Skaha & Okanagan Falls
regions.summary: A cooler stretch around Skaha Lake and Okanagan Falls, with granite and limestone benches ideal for Pinot Noir and Riesling.

regions.name: Naramata Bench
regions.summary: A terraced bench on the east shore of Okanagan Lake, with a lake influence and some of the valley's most celebrated boutique wineries.

regions.name: Kelowna & Lake Country
regions.summary: Around the city of Kelowna and the north shore: a cooler area for aromatic whites, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Similkameen Valley
regions.summary: A narrow, windy valley west of the Okanagan, around Keremeos. Many organic vineyards on stony soil, and wines with natural freshness.

regions.name: Fraser Valley
regions.summary: A cool, rainy coastal valley east of Vancouver: aromatic whites and light reds.

regions.name: Vancouver Island
regions.summary: Cowichan Valley and the island south of Nanaimo: cool and maritime, with lively whites and Pinot Noir, and many small wineries.

regions.name: Gulf Islands
regions.summary: Sheltered islands in the Strait of Georgia (Salt Spring, Pender, Saturna) with a Mediterranean-like mild climate.

regions.name: China
regions.summary: Now among the world's top ten wine producers and the second-largest vineyard area in the world (mostly table grapes). Ningxia in the north-west is the quality leader, with Cabernet Gernischt, Marselan and Cabernet Sauvignon grown in winter-buried vines.
regions.climate: Mostly continental, with huge winter cold: vines must be buried every winter in Ningxia and Xinjiang.
regions.styles: Rich Cabernet blends in Ningxia, fresh whites in Shandong, ice wine in the north-east and fortified wines in Shanxi.
regions.classification: The main wine regions are Ningxia, Shandong, Hebei, Xinjiang, Yunnan, Shanxi and Gansu, plus Liaoning and Jilin for ice wine.
regions.history: Grape wine was drunk in Xinjiang from at least the Han dynasty. Zhang Bishi founded the first big modern winery, Changyu, in Yantai in 1892.
facts: In 2011 Chateau Helan Mountain's Ningxia Cabernet beat Bordeaux in an international competition in Decanter.
Vineyards in Ningxia are buried under 30–50 cm of soil each winter to survive temperatures of -25°C.

regions.name: Ningxia
regions.summary: China's most celebrated region: the foot of the Helan Mountain near Yinchuan, with gravel, sunny days and cold nights, producing elegant Cabernet blends.
regions.climate: Dry continental, with 3,000 hours of sunshine.

regions.name: Helan Mountain East
regions.summary: The strip of vineyards on the alluvial fans east of the Helan mountains, the best area of Ningxia, with more than 100 wineries.

regions.name: Shandong
regions.summary: The Yantai–Penglai peninsula on the Yellow Sea: the oldest modern wine area, with a mild maritime climate and the home of Changyu.

regions.name: Hebei & Beijing
regions.summary: Huailai and Changli, within reach of Beijing: sunny, dry vineyards on the Guanting basin and the coast.

regions.name: Xinjiang
regions.summary: A huge, dry and sunny north-west, with grapes grown for centuries around Turpan; modern wineries near Manas and Yili.

regions.name: Yunnan
regions.summary: High Tibetan-edge vineyards near Shangri-La and Deqin at 2,000 to 2,600 m, tended in terraces by local villagers.

regions.name: Shanxi & Gansu
regions.summary: The dry north-central plateau with the Taiyuan basin and the Hexi corridor (Wuwei): high, dry vineyards with a long summer.

regions.name: North-East (ice wine)
regions.summary: Cold northern provinces making ice wine from frozen Vidal and native mountain grapes.

regions.name: Yongning (Yinchuan)
regions.summary: The core of Ningxia's Helan Mountain East: gravelly fans just south-west of Yinchuan, home to many of the best-known estates.
regions.climate: Very dry, 3,000 sunshine hours; vines are buried under soil in winter.

regions.name: Shizuishan
regions.summary: The northern end of the Helan Mountain East belt, on sandy, stony soils.

regions.name: Qingtongxia
regions.summary: A warm, sunny area on the Yellow River with sandy soils, known for ripe reds and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Hongsibu
regions.summary: A hot, dry, high-altitude area with sandy desert soils at the southern end of Ningxia's wine belt.

regions.name: Penglai
regions.summary: A coastal peninsula tip on the Bohai and Yellow Seas, with sandy and gravelly vineyards, a cluster of top estates and the 'Penglai Wine Coast'.
regions.climate: Maritime, with warm autumns and summer monsoon rain.

regions.name: Yantai
regions.summary: China's oldest modern wine city, where Changyu was founded in 1892.

regions.name: Longkou & Zhaoyuan
regions.summary: The western Yantai district, with the hills of the Jiaodong peninsula and sandy loams.

regions.name: Weihai
regions.summary: The easternmost tip of the peninsula, cool and sea-washed, growing white wine grapes.

regions.name: Laixi (Qingdao)
regions.summary: A small area near Qingdao with Chardonnay and Riesling for sparkling and still wines.

regions.name: Huailai
regions.summary: The Guanting basin north-west of Beijing: high, dry, sunny vineyards on sandy soils, with Chateau Changyu-Rongchen and others.
regions.climate: Dry, with big day-night swings at 500 m.

regions.name: Changli
regions.summary: A coastal area at the foot of the Yanshan mountains near the Bohai Sea, producing Cabernet and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Yanqing (Beijing)
regions.summary: Beijing's own wine district, on the north-west side of the capital.

regions.name: Turpan
regions.summary: The oasis below sea level where grapes have been grown for over 2,000 years, mostly for raisins and table fruit.
regions.climate: Among the hottest, driest places in China.

regions.name: Manas & Shihezi
regions.summary: The north side of the Tianshan mountains: a cooler, quality-focused area with dry, sunny vineyards.
regions.climate: Continental; vines are buried in winter.

regions.name: Yili Valley
regions.summary: A green valley near Kazakhstan with higher rainfall and cool nights, planted with Riesling and Cabernet.

regions.name: Hami
regions.summary: An eastern Xinjiang oasis town known for sweet melons and increasingly for wine grapes.

regions.name: Shangri-La
regions.summary: Terraced Tibetan villages in the Mekong and Yangtze river gorges at 2,200 to 2,600 m: Cabernet Sauvignon and the local 'Rose Honey' grape.
regions.climate: High and dry in winter; very strong UV.

regions.name: Mile
regions.summary: A warm, sunny area in south-central Yunnan, source of the first Yunnan table wines.

regions.name: Binchuan
regions.summary: A sunny basin near Dali with a long season.

regions.name: Taiyuan Basin
regions.summary: Qingxu and the Fen river basin in Shanxi, a place of stony, high-altitude vineyards (Grace Vineyard).

regions.name: Wuwei (Hexi Corridor)
regions.summary: A desert corridor along the old Silk Road, with irrigated vineyards between the Qilian mountains and the Gobi.
regions.climate: Hot and dry with huge temperature swings.

regions.name: Jiuquan
regions.summary: A remote Silk Road oasis with desert vineyards.

regions.name: Tonghua
regions.summary: Jilin's ice wine heartland: Vidal and local mountain grapes frozen on the vine at -8 C.
regions.climate: Very cold winters, short summers.

regions.name: Huanren
regions.summary: Liaoning's best ice wine area, on the Yalu river side, producing ice wines from Vidal.

regions.name: Ji'an
regions.summary: A border town on the Yalu river in Jilin, one of the three Jilin ice wine areas.

regions.name: Croatia
regions.summary: A long coast and a continental interior with 130 native grapes: Istria's Malvazija, the Dalmatian Plavac Mali (a close cousin of Zinfandel) and Slavonian oak for the world.
regions.climate: Mediterranean on the Adriatic coast and islands; cooler continental in the north and east.
regions.styles: Dry, fresh whites (Malvazija, Pošip, Graševina), rich reds from Plavac Mali and the island of Vis, and sweet wines such as Prošek.
regions.classification: Four wine regions (Slavonia & Croatian Danube, Plateau, Istria & Kvarner, Dalmatia) split into sub-regions and about 66 appellations.
regions.history: Greeks planted vines on Adriatic islands in the 4th century BC. DNA tests in 2001 showed that Zinfandel in California is the same grape as Crljenak Kaštelanski from Dalmatia, and Plavac Mali is its offspring.
facts: Dingač on the Pelješac peninsula was the first protected wine region in Yugoslavia (1961).
Slavonian oak from Croatia's eastern forests is prized for barrels worldwide.

regions.name: Slavonia & the Danube
regions.summary: The eastern lowlands, between the Sava and Drava rivers and the Danube: the home of Graševina, a floral, easy white that is Croatia's most planted grape.

regions.name: Plateau (Continental Croatia)
regions.summary: The cool hills around Zagreb and the Slovenian border: crisp whites and sparkling wines, especially from Plešivica and Međimurje.

regions.name: Istria & Kvarner
regions.summary: The north Adriatic peninsula with red 'terra rossa' soil: very fresh Malvazija, the white grape of Istria, and earthy Teran.

regions.name: Dalmatia
regions.summary: The long Adriatic coast and its islands: sun-baked limestone slopes growing powerful Plavac Mali reds and mineral whites.
regions.climate: Mediterranean, with hot summers and mild winters.

regions.name: Istria
regions.summary: A green peninsula with Italian influence: Malvazija from 'terra rossa' soil is Croatia's most exciting white.

regions.name: Pelješac Peninsula
regions.summary: A rocky peninsula with the famous Dingač and Postup slopes, where Plavac Mali on steep, sun-drenched terraces by the sea makes Croatia's most powerful reds.

regions.name: Central Dalmatia & islands
regions.summary: The Split coast and the islands of Hvar, Brač, Vis and Korčula, with the oldest vines on the Adriatic.

regions.name: Cyprus
regions.summary: The home of Commandaria, one of the world's oldest named wines (since the 12th century), and Xynisteri and Mavro grapes grown among Troodos mountain villages.
regions.climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean summers; the best vineyards climb the Troodos mountains to 1,500 m.
regions.styles: Dry whites from Xynisteri, red Maratheftiko, and the sweet, raisined Commandaria.
regions.classification: Regional PDO and PGI areas such as Commandaria, Laona-Akamas, Pitsilia, Krasochoria and Vouni Panagias-Ambelitis.
regions.history: Cyprus has made wine for 6,000 years. Commandaria was served at the wedding of Richard the Lionheart in 1191 and is thought to be the oldest still-made wine.
facts: Many Cypriot vines are old, ungrafted bush vines, as phylloxera never arrived on the island.
Commandaria is made from sun-dried Xynisteri and Mavro grapes in 14 villages of the Limassol mountains.

regions.name: Limassol & the southern Troodos
regions.summary: The wine heart of the island: mountain villages such as Omodos and Laneia above the coast, with old bush vines on chalk and volcanic soils at 600 to 1,500 m.

regions.name: Commandaria
regions.summary: A zone of 14 villages in the Limassol foothills, making sweet, dark Commandaria from sun-dried grapes, the world's oldest named wine.

regions.name: Paphos & Laona-Akamas
regions.summary: The wild west of Cyprus, with Laona, Akamas and the Paphos highlands: the home of the red Maratheftiko and rare local white grapes.

regions.name: Nicosia & Pitsilia
regions.summary: The central plain and the northern Troodos slopes, with the cool, high-altitude Pitsilia area.

regions.name: Larnaca
regions.summary: The eastern coast, with some old vineyards in the Vouni Panagias area and a long winemaking tradition.

regions.name: England & Wales
regions.summary: The world's fastest-growing cool-climate wine country, led by sparkling wine from chalk soils that run under the English Channel to Champagne.
regions.climate: Cool and maritime. Warmer summers than a generation ago have made ripening more reliable, but spring frost and wet summers are the main risks.
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling wine from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier (the Champagne grapes), plus aromatic still whites such as Bacchus.
regions.classification: Protected designations of origin (PDO): Sussex, Darnibbles, Essex, Cornwall, Hampshire (as English Sparkling), plus 'English Wine' and 'Welsh Wine' as national categories.
regions.history: The Romans planted vines here, and monks kept some going in the Middle Ages. The modern industry began in Hampshire in the 1950s; in 2018 vineyards covered more than 3,000 hectares.
facts: Ground in Kent, Sussex and Hampshire is the same Cretaceous chalk as Champagne, about 150 km away across the Channel.
Many Champagne houses, such as Taittinger, have planted vineyards in England.

regions.name: South-East England
regions.summary: The heartland of English sparkling wine: chalk downs and greensand ridges, a warm, sunny corner of the country, with most of the best-known producers.
regions.climate: The warmest and driest part of England.

regions.name: Kent
regions.summary: The Garden of England, with chalk on the North Downs and some of the largest vineyards, such as Chapel Down. Excellent sparkling wine.

regions.name: Sussex
regions.summary: The first English region with its own protected designation (PDO Sussex, 2022), on the South Downs. Home of Nyetimber, Ridgeview and Rathfinny.

regions.name: Surrey
regions.summary: The North Downs of Surrey, just outside London, with the chalk and flint of Denbies, England's biggest single vineyard.

regions.name: Hampshire & Isle of Wight
regions.summary: Where modern English wine began (Hambledon, 1952). Chalk downland with some of the warmest sites; Hattingley and Exton Park.

regions.name: Thames Valley & Chilterns
regions.summary: The Chilterns and Thames valley west of London, a growing area of chalk vineyards.

regions.name: East of England
regions.summary: The driest, sunniest part of Britain: flat, open land where aromatic whites and sparkling wines are grown.
regions.climate: Dry and sunny, but cooler in spring, with a frost risk.

regions.name: Essex
regions.summary: A PDO region on clay soils that give structured still wines as well as sparkling.

regions.name: Norfolk & Suffolk
regions.summary: East Anglian vineyards close to the North Sea, producing crisp Bacchus and sparkling wine.

regions.name: South-West England
regions.summary: A mild, wet maritime region with south-facing slopes: sparkling wine in Cornwall and Dorset, aromatic whites in Devon and Somerset.

regions.name: Cornwall
regions.summary: A protected designation at England's south-western tip, with mild winters and sea breezes.

regions.name: Devon, Dorset & Somerset
regions.summary: The Jurassic coast and Somerset levels: rolling hills with a long tradition of cider, now also making sparkling and aromatic wine.

regions.name: Wiltshire & Gloucestershire
regions.summary: Cotswold limestone and the Severn vale, home of some of the oldest vineyards in the country.

regions.name: Midlands & the North
regions.summary: The cooler, wetter centre and north, where early-ripening varieties such as Solaris succeed in sheltered sites.

regions.name: Wales
regions.summary: Around 20 vineyards, most in the south and west, from the Vale of Glamorgan and Monmouthshire to Pembrokeshire. Mild, wet and breezy; Welsh Wine is its own protected category.

regions.name: Georgia
regions.summary: The cradle of wine: 8,000 years of winemaking, ancient clay-vessel (qvevri) wines, amber whites and more than 500 native grape varieties.
regions.climate: Subtropical in the west (Black Sea), continental in the east, with the Greater Caucasus shielding the vineyards from the north.
regions.styles: Two traditions side by side: European-style fresh whites and reds, and the ancient method where grapes ferment with their skins in buried clay qvevri, giving amber (orange) wines, tannic and savory.
regions.classification: Georgia has about 25 protected designations of origin (PDO, 'appellations'), nearly all in the east: Tsinandali, Mukuzani, Kindzmarauli, Khvanchkara, Tvishi, Sviri, Ojaleshi and more. Zones drawn here follow the municipality of each appellation and a ring around the named villages, so edges are approximate.
regions.history: Archaeologists found 8,000-year-old wine residue in clay jars in southern Georgia, the oldest known evidence of winemaking. Vines are woven into Georgian culture, and the traditional qvevri method is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
facts: Saperavi is a rare red grape with red flesh as well as red skin, so its wines are inky and long-lived.
Qvevri are egg-shaped clay jars buried to the neck, used for fermenting, ageing and storing the wine.
A Georgian feast (supra) has a toastmaster (tamada) who leads the toasts.

regions.name: Kakheti
regions.summary: The heart of Georgian wine, in the east at the foot of the Caucasus: about 70% of all Georgian wine, from fresh whites to qvevri amber wines and dark Saperavi.
regions.climate: Continental with long, warm summers and cold winters; the mountains to the north protect the vines from cold winds.
regions.styles: Amber Rkatsiteli aged in qvevri, off-dry reds like Kindzmarauli, and fresh European-style whites.

regions.name: Telavi district
regions.summary: Around the town of Telavi: home of the Tsinandali (white), Mukuzani (red), Napareuli, Teliani and Kardenakhi designations. Mukuzani is a classic oaked Saperavi.

regions.name: Gurjaani district
regions.summary: A big grape-growing area in central Kakheti, with the Gurjaani, Vazisubani and Manavi designations. Fresh, mineral whites, many made in qvevri.

regions.name: Kvareli district
regions.summary: North-east Kakheti, below the mountains: home of Kindzmarauli, the best-known off-dry red, soft and velvety, with dark cherry and pomegranate.

regions.name: Sighnaghi district
regions.summary: The hilltop wine town on the border with Azerbaijan, with views across the Alazani valley; many small qvevri producers.

regions.name: Sagarejo district
regions.summary: Western Kakheti, a mix of vineyards and forest: the Manavi and Tibaani areas, known for their lively whites.

regions.name: Lagodekhi & Akhmeta
regions.summary: The north-east and north-west edges of Kakheti, with cool mountain air: the home of the rare, delicate Khikhvi.

regions.name: Kartli
regions.summary: The central plain around Tbilisi and Gori: light, fresh whites from Goruli Mtsvane and Chinuri, traditional-method sparkling wines and the red Tavkveri.
regions.climate: Continental, drier and cooler than Kakheti.

regions.name: Imereti
regions.summary: Western Georgia, around Kutaisi: softer, lighter whites with less skin contact than Kakheti. Tsitska and Tsolikouri are the stars.
regions.climate: Humid subtropical with plenty of rain.

regions.name: Racha-Lechkhumi
regions.summary: A remote mountain region in the north-west, famous for Khvanchkara: a naturally semi-sweet red from Alexandrouli and Mujuretuli, scented with raspberry and spice.
regions.climate: Cool, mountain climate with long autumns.

regions.name: Samegrelo
regions.summary: Near the Black Sea in the north-west: the home of the red Ojaleshi, a light, fruity wine, and a lush, green landscape.

regions.name: Guria & Adjara
regions.summary: The wet Black Sea coast, with tiny plots of the rare Chkhaveri, which makes pink, high-acid wines.

regions.name: Meskheti
regions.summary: A high, cool plateau in the south-west, mostly mountain pasture, with a small revived wine tradition.

regions.name: Tsinandali
regions.summary: The first Georgian appellation (1919): a dry, fresh white blend of Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane, grown near Prince Chavchavadze's estate. Drawn as an approximate zone around the village.

regions.name: Napareuli
regions.summary: A village appellation on the right bank of the Alazani river, known for sturdy Saperavi and full-bodied Rkatsiteli. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Mukuzani
regions.summary: The classic dry red of Kakheti: 100% Saperavi from south-facing slopes, aged in oak, with dark fruit, spice and ageing potential. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Vazisubani
regions.summary: A white-wine appellation of Gurjaani, with Rkatsiteli, Mtsvane and Kisi on sandy and clay soils. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Akhasheni
regions.summary: A semi-sweet red made from Saperavi, stopped before it is fully fermented, with ripe cherry and spice. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Kindzmarauli
regions.summary: The best-known semi-sweet red in Georgia, made from Saperavi grown on steep south-facing slopes: velvety, with dark cherry and pomegranate. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Kardenakhi
regions.summary: A fortified-style dessert wine area of Kvareli; the name also means a strong, rich white. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Sviri
regions.summary: A white appellation near Zestafoni and Terjola, using Tsolikouri and Tsitska. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Khvanchkara
regions.summary: Georgia's most famous semi-sweet red, from steep terraces by Ambrolauri: Alexandrouli and Mujuretuli, with raspberry, spice and a gentle sweetness. Said to be Stalin's favourite wine.

regions.name: Tvishi
regions.summary: A rare, naturally sweet white from Tsolikouri grown in Lechkhumi. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Ojaleshi
regions.summary: A light, fruity red from the Ojaleshi grape (Samegrelo): red berries and spice, with fresh acidity. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Atenuri
regions.summary: A white and sparkling-wine zone in the Atenuri gorge near Gori, with the Chinuri grape for traditional-method sparkling wine. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Great Lakes & Midwest
regions.summary: Cool-climate wine on the shores of the Great Lakes (Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania) and up the Mississippi: Riesling, Pinot Gris, ice wine and hardy hybrids.
regions.climate: Cold winters and warm summers, softened by the huge lakes whose water releases heat in autumn and delays spring.
regions.styles: Dry and off-dry Riesling, ice wine, sparkling wine, and Norton, a native grape with deep colour.
regions.classification: American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) such as Leelanau Peninsula, Old Mission Peninsula, Lake Erie and Ohio River Valley.
facts: The Leelanau and Old Mission peninsulas in Michigan sit on the 45th parallel, the same latitude as Bordeaux and the Piedmont.
Missouri's Hermann was the first AVA in the United States, in 1980.

regions.name: Leelanau Peninsula
regions.summary: A narrow peninsula in north-west Michigan with Lake Michigan on three sides. Some of the best Riesling and Pinot Gris of the Midwest.

regions.name: Old Mission Peninsula
regions.summary: A 19-mile finger of land in Grand Traverse Bay: cool, breezy vineyards with ripe whites and clean, lean reds.

regions.name: Lake Michigan Shore
regions.summary: Michigan's south-west corner, on sand dunes with lake-moderated weather. The state's oldest wine region.

regions.name: Fennville
regions.summary: A small AVA inland from Lake Michigan, in fruit-growing country.

regions.name: Tip of the Mitt
regions.summary: Michigan's far north: cold-hardy grapes among the resort towns of Lake Huron.

regions.name: Lake Erie (Great Lakes)
regions.summary: A big, long AVA along the south shore of Lake Erie across Ohio, Pennsylvania and New York: the biggest grape region in the east, from Concord juice grapes to quality ice wine.

regions.name: Grand River Valley
regions.summary: North-east Ohio, near Lake Erie: cool and snowy winters, producing aromatic whites and ice wine.

regions.name: Ohio River Valley
regions.summary: The enormous, historic AVA along the Ohio River across Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky and West Virginia. Cincinnati was once the biggest wine town in the US, famous for Catawba sparkling wine.

regions.name: Indiana Uplands
regions.summary: Limestone hills in southern Indiana with small family wineries.

regions.name: Hermann
regions.summary: The first AVA in the United States (1980), in the Missouri River valley. German settlers made it the centre of the Norton grape.

regions.name: Augusta
regions.summary: America's very first AVA (1980), in the Missouri River hills above St. Louis, with Norton as the star.

regions.name: Ozark Highlands
regions.summary: A cool, hilly area in southern Missouri with old Norton plantings.

regions.name: Shawnee Hills
regions.summary: Southern Illinois hills with a wine trail among the forests.

regions.name: Upper Mississippi River Valley
regions.summary: A huge AVA across Wisconsin, Minnesota, Illinois and Iowa along the river, where cold-hardy hybrids thrive.

regions.name: Wisconsin Ledge
regions.summary: Door County and the limestone cliffs of eastern Wisconsin, softened by Lake Michigan.

regions.name: Lake Wisconsin
regions.summary: A small AVA near Madison with cool-climate hybrids.

regions.name: Japan
regions.summary: A very small but beautiful wine industry, built on Koshu, a pale pink grape grown in Yamanashi for over 1,000 years, and on increasingly serious wines from Nagano and Hokkaido.
regions.climate: Humid with typhoon rain in summer, so vines are trained overhead (pergola style) to keep the grapes dry.
regions.styles: Delicate, citrusy Koshu, fresh whites, light reds and fine sparkling wine.
regions.classification: Japan Wine (made only from grapes grown in Japan) and Geographical Indications for Yamanashi, Hokkaido, Nagano and Yamagata.
regions.history: Legend says the Buddhist monk Gyoki brought Koshu in 718 AD. Modern winemaking began in Yamanashi in 1877.
facts: Koshu is grown on tall pergolas to avoid rot in Japan's rain and humidity.
Only wines made entirely from grapes grown in Japan may be called Japan Wine (nihon wain).

regions.name: Yamanashi
regions.summary: The cradle of Japanese wine, west of Tokyo under Mount Fuji: about 30% of Japan's wineries. Koshu grown at Katsunuma makes delicate, citrus-fresh whites.

regions.name: Nagano
regions.summary: The Japan Alps: cool, high vineyards at 600 to 800 m and Merlot from Kikyogahara and Chikuma River. Japan's second-biggest wine area.

regions.name: Hokkaido
regions.summary: The cool northern island of Yoichi and Furano: Germanic whites, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine in a climate like Alsace.

regions.name: Yamagata & the north
regions.summary: Tohoku and the Sea of Japan coast: Yamagata's Tendo and Kaminoyama make crisp whites and reds.

regions.name: Kansai & the west
regions.summary: Western Japan, with older vineyards in Osaka (Kashiwara) and small wineries.

regions.name: Kantō & central Honshu
regions.summary: The hills around Tokyo and the central Alps, with boutique winemakers like those of Tochigi's Coco Farm.

regions.name: Baja California
regions.summary: Mexico's best-known wine region: a Mediterranean-like peninsula with a thriving food and wine scene around the Valle de Guadalupe, 90 minutes south of San Diego. It makes about 70–90% of Mexican wine.
regions.climate: Mediterranean: dry, sunny summers and cool nights from the Pacific, with winter rain.
regions.styles: Bold Cabernet-based blends and Rhône or Italian varieties, with fresh whites such as Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin.
regions.classification: No national appellation system yet; wineries label by valley: Valle de Guadalupe, Valle de Santo Tomás, Ojos Negros, San Vicente and Tecate.
regions.history: Spanish Dominican missionaries planted Mission grapes in the 1700s, and Russian Molokan settlers brought winemaking to Guadalupe in the early 20th century.
facts: Baja California is the oldest and biggest wine region in Mexico by far.
Valle de Guadalupe has more than 150 wineries within about 30 km.

regions.name: Valle de Guadalupe
regions.summary: The flagship valley, with a Mediterranean climate and granite and alluvial soils, 20 km from the Pacific. Home of the best-known wineries and restaurants.

regions.name: Valle de Ojos Negros
regions.summary: A higher, cooler basin north-east of Ensenada, with cold nights and big temperature swings.

regions.name: Valle de Santo Tomás
regions.summary: The site of Baja's first mission vineyards (1791), home to historic wineries.

regions.name: Valle de San Vicente
regions.summary: A small, southern valley with a cooler climate from the coast, and a growing set of boutique wineries.

regions.name: Tecate
regions.summary: On the US border, a dry, warm area of vineyards and small wineries.

regions.name: Rest of Baja California
regions.summary: The rest of the northern peninsula, including the cities of Tijuana and Ensenada.

regions.name: Mexico
regions.summary: The oldest wine country in the Americas: Hernán Cortés ordered vines planted in 1524, and Casa Madero in Parras (1597) is the oldest winery in the Americas. Today the high plateau and the north produce a growing quality wine scene.
regions.climate: High plateau, dry and sunny, with cool nights at 1,500 to 2,000 m.
regions.styles: Bold, ripe reds, fresh whites and growing sparkling wine, from the same latitude as the Canaries.
regions.classification: No national appellation system: wineries label by valley (Valle de Parras, Querétaro, Guanajuato, Zacatecas…). The Valle de Guadalupe is on its own map (Baja California).
facts: In 1699 the Spanish crown banned wine production in the New World to protect Spanish exports; missions kept making sacramental wine.
Querétaro is Mexico's second-biggest wine area, with a big sparkling wine tradition near Tequisquiapan.

regions.name: Coahuila & Parras
regions.summary: The oldest wine area in the Americas, at the high desert around Parras de la Fuente, home of Casa Madero (1597).

regions.name: Querétaro
regions.summary: A plateau at 1,700 to 2,000 m, with the Freixenet and Cava-style sparkling houses, and Bernal and Tequisquiapan wine routes.

regions.name: Guanajuato
regions.summary: Mexico's high colonial heartland, near San Miguel de Allende and Dolores Hidalgo: a fast-growing wine route.

regions.name: Zacatecas & Aguascalientes
regions.summary: High, dry plains of the central highlands, with vineyards at nearly 2,000 m.

regions.name: Chihuahua, Durango & Nuevo León
regions.summary: Scattered vineyards in the northern states, from the Chihuahuan desert to the Sierra Madre.

regions.name: Virginia & the Mid-Atlantic
regions.summary: Thomas Jefferson's dream: Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and West Virginia make elegant Viognier, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Chardonnay in a warm, humid climate.
regions.climate: Warm, humid summers and cold winters. Rain at harvest is the main risk, so growers pick well-drained slopes.
regions.styles: Viognier (Virginia's signature white), Bordeaux-style reds led by Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, sparkling wine and sweet Riesling.
regions.classification: American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) such as Monticello, Shenandoah Valley, Lehigh Valley and Outer Coastal Plain.
regions.history: Jefferson planted European vines at Monticello in the 1770s but they died of disease; modern Virginia wine took off in the 1970s. The native grape Norton is called Virginia's grape.
facts: Virginia has more than 300 wineries, a leading wine state on the East Coast.
Viognier was chosen as Virginia's official state grape in 2011.

regions.name: Monticello
regions.summary: Around Charlottesville and Jefferson's home: red clay hills where Viognier and Cabernet Franc do best. Home of the first Virginia AVA (1984).

regions.name: Shenandoah Valley
regions.summary: A long valley between the Blue Ridge and the Alleghenies across Virginia and West Virginia, with limestone soils and cooler nights.

regions.name: Middleburg
regions.summary: Horse country west of Washington DC: high, well-drained hills and elegant Bordeaux-style blends.

regions.name: Northern Neck
regions.summary: A peninsula of the Chesapeake region where George Washington was born: warm, maritime and mostly Bordeaux varieties.

regions.name: Virginia Peninsula
regions.summary: A small, flat AVA at Virginia's old colonial heart (Jamestown, Williamsburg).

regions.name: Virginia's Eastern Shore
regions.summary: A sandy finger of land between the Atlantic and the Chesapeake Bay with sea breezes and an extended season.

regions.name: North Fork of Roanoke
regions.summary: An upland valley in south-west Virginia with a cooler climate and mountain views.

regions.name: Rocky Knob
regions.summary: A tiny, high-altitude AVA along the Blue Ridge Parkway with cool, long ripening.

regions.name: Appalachian High Country
regions.summary: A mountain AVA across North Carolina, Virginia and Tennessee: vineyards from 2,500 ft up, with cold winters.

regions.name: Yadkin Valley
regions.summary: North Carolina's first and largest AVA, in the Piedmont: warm days and ripe reds.

regions.name: Catoctin
regions.summary: A ridge in northern Maryland with slate soils and good drainage.

regions.name: Linganore
regions.summary: Maryland's rolling piedmont, with some of the state's oldest wineries.

regions.name: Cumberland Valley
regions.summary: A valley across Maryland and Pennsylvania with limestone-rich soils.

regions.name: Lancaster Valley
regions.summary: Pennsylvania's Amish country, with calcium-rich soils.

regions.name: Lehigh Valley
regions.summary: Pennsylvania's north-east, on the slopes of the Blue Mountain: fresh whites and growing quality.

regions.name: Central Delaware Valley
regions.summary: On both sides of the Delaware River between Pennsylvania and New Jersey, with river air that cools the vines.

regions.name: Outer Coastal Plain
regions.summary: Southern New Jersey: sandy soils and a long ripening season under maritime influence.

regions.name: Warren Hills
regions.summary: New Jersey's cool north-west hills, on limestone and shale.

regions.name: Kanawha River Valley
regions.summary: A river AVA in West Virginia with deep, well-drained soil beside the river.

regions.name: Moldova
regions.summary: One of the most vine-covered countries per head in the world, famous for vast underground cellars (Mileștii Mici has 200 km of tunnels) and a revival of Fetească and Rară Neagră.
regions.climate: Temperate continental, mild and sunny, with long summers and hard winters.
regions.styles: Simple fruity whites, sparkling wine made in underground cellars, and richer reds from Fetească Neagră and Rară Neagră.
regions.classification: Three PGI regions (Valul lui Traian, Ștefan Vodă, Codru) plus Divin (brandy) and PDO regions such as Codru, Ștefan Vodă and Valul lui Traian.
regions.history: Wine has been made on the land between the Carpathians and the Dniester for over 3,000 years. In the 1800s Moldovan wine reached the tsars' tables, and under the Soviet Union Moldova supplied wine to the whole union. Since 2005 Russia's wine bans pushed producers to the EU and new markets.
facts: The Mileștii Mici cellar holds the biggest wine collection in the world (almost 2 million bottles) in tunnels 85 m below ground.
Wine has long been Moldova's top export, with the former Soviet Union as its main market.

regions.name: Codru
regions.summary: The wooded hills of central Moldova around Chișinău, the heart of the wine industry. It holds the famous Cricova and Mileștii Mici cellars.

regions.name: Ștefan Vodă
regions.summary: The south-east, near the Dniester river and the Black Sea: warm days and ripe reds.

regions.name: Valul lui Traian
regions.summary: Named after the Trajan's Wall earthworks, the hot, dry south, known for full-bodied reds and Muscat.

regions.name: North Moldova
regions.summary: A cooler, hillier part of the country, with fewer vineyards.

regions.name: Cricova
regions.summary: A wine town just north of Chișinău with 120 km of limestone tunnels (the old quarries) used as a cellar for sparkling wines and a famous underground tasting road. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Mileștii Mici
regions.summary: The 'Golden Collection' cellar: 200 km of tunnels in limestone, the biggest wine collection in the world (almost 2 million bottles). Approximate zone.

regions.name: Purcari
regions.summary: Moldova's most prized red area, near the Dniester river: a favourite of 19th-century tsars. Famous for a Bordeaux-style blend, and for Negru de Purcari. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Ceadîr-Lunga (Gagauzia)
regions.summary: The Gagauz autonomous area in the south, with hot, dry summers that ripen full-bodied reds. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Romănești
regions.summary: A traditional vineyard village west of Chișinău in the heart of Codru, known for fresh white wines. Approximate zone.

regions.name: Idaho & Colorado
regions.summary: Vineyards at serious altitude: Idaho's Snake River Valley and Colorado's high Western Slope grow Syrah, Riesling, Cabernet and Merlot at 1,500 to 6,000 feet.
regions.climate: High, dry continental climate: hot days, cold nights and winter freezes that make site choice critical.
regions.styles: Syrah, Riesling, Tempranillo and Bordeaux reds, with fresh, bright whites.
regions.classification: American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) such as Snake River Valley, Eagle Foothills, Grand Valley and West Elks.
facts: Colorado's Grand Valley is among the highest-altitude wine regions in the world, at about 4,500 to 6,400 ft.
The Snake River Valley AVA shares a border with Oregon and is the Pacific Northwest's third wine hub after Washington and Oregon.

regions.name: Snake River Valley
regions.summary: Idaho's big wine region, in the Snake River plain from Boise to the Oregon border. High-desert sunshine, cool nights and volcanic-ash soils.

regions.name: Eagle Foothills
regions.summary: A hillside AVA north of Boise at 2,600 to 3,000 ft, with slopes that sit above the frosty valley floor.

regions.name: Lewis-Clark Valley
regions.summary: Idaho's lowest, warmest wine area, in a deep river canyon at the Washington border.

regions.name: Grand Valley
regions.summary: Colorado's main wine region around Grand Junction on the Western Slope, at about 4,500 ft, with orchards as well as vines.

regions.name: West Elks
regions.summary: One of America's highest AVAs at around 6,000 ft, in cool Colorado hills near Paonia.

regions.name: New York & New England
regions.summary: America's oldest wine state and its cool-climate frontier: Riesling and Cabernet Franc by the Finger Lakes, maritime vines on Long Island and tiny, determined vineyards across New England.
regions.climate: Cool continental. The big lakes (and on Long Island the Atlantic) soften the winter cold and delay spring, so vines escape frost.
regions.styles: Crisp, aromatic Riesling (dry to sweet, including ice wine), elegant Cabernet Franc and Merlot, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.
regions.classification: American Viticultural Areas (AVAs), such as Finger Lakes and Long Island. New York also has its own 'Appellation' rules for labelling.
regions.history: Vines have grown here since Dutch settlers in the 1600s. In 1962 Konstantin Frank, a Ukrainian immigrant, proved that European Vitis vinifera such as Riesling could survive Finger Lakes winters.
facts: New York is the third-largest wine-producing state, after California and Washington.
The Finger Lakes are deep glacial lakes: Seneca Lake never freezes and warms the vineyards around it.

regions.name: Finger Lakes
regions.summary: The state's flagship region: long, narrow glacial lakes with steep slopes of vines above the water. Riesling is the star, from bone-dry to sweet, with fine Cabernet Franc and sparkling wine.
regions.climate: Cool continental, moderated by deep lakes that store summer heat and release it in autumn.

regions.name: Seneca Lake
regions.summary: The deepest Finger Lake and the one that holds the most wineries: powerful Riesling and Chardonnay from slopes on both shores.

regions.name: Cayuga Lake
regions.summary: The first wine trail in America: shale slopes above the longest Finger Lake, with elegant Riesling and Cabernet Franc.

regions.name: Long Island
regions.summary: A maritime region two hours from New York City. Sea breezes and a long season give Bordeaux-style reds led by Merlot, plus fresh whites.
regions.climate: Maritime, with long autumns tempered by the Atlantic and Long Island Sound.

regions.name: North Fork
regions.summary: The long, narrow peninsula with water on both sides, home of most Long Island wineries: Merlot, Cabernet Franc and clean, crisp whites.

regions.name: The Hamptons
regions.summary: The south fork, famous for its summer homes: a smaller group of vineyards on fertile, sandy soil with mild, maritime weather.

regions.name: Hudson River Region
regions.summary: The oldest continuous wine region in the United States (since 1677), in the Hudson Valley north of New York City: French-American hybrids and growing plantings of Cabernet Franc.

regions.name: Upper Hudson
regions.summary: A cold, small AVA near Saratoga, where very hardy hybrids such as Marquette and Frontenac survive hard winters.

regions.name: Champlain Valley
regions.summary: The state's northernmost wine area, by Lake Champlain, growing cold-hardy grapes bred in Minnesota and Cornell.

regions.name: Lake Erie
regions.summary: A long strip along the shore of Lake Erie across New York, Pennsylvania and Ohio. The biggest grape-growing region in the east, mostly Concord for juice, with growing quality wine.
regions.climate: Lake-effect snow insulates the vines, and the water delays spring.

regions.name: Niagara Escarpment
regions.summary: A limestone ridge on the south shore of Lake Ontario, the same escarpment that makes the nearby Ontario wines: fresh whites and light reds.

regions.name: Southeastern New England
regions.summary: Coastal Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts: a mild, maritime strip for crisp whites, sparkling wine and light reds.
regions.climate: Maritime, with sea breezes that moderate the cold winters.

regions.name: Martha's Vineyard
regions.summary: An island AVA south of Cape Cod: a few vineyards that make clean, salty-fresh Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Western Connecticut Highlands
regions.summary: Hills in north-west Connecticut with cool nights and well-drained slopes, planted with Chardonnay and French-American hybrids.

regions.name: Eastern Connecticut Highlands
regions.summary: The rolling eastern uplands of Connecticut: small wineries with aromatic whites and light reds.

regions.name: Oregon & Washington
regions.summary: The Pacific Northwest: Oregon's cool, green Willamette Valley is the New World's Pinot Noir capital, while Washington's desert vineyards make bold Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah and Riesling.
regions.climate: West of the Cascade Mountains the climate is cool and rainy; east of them it is a hot, dry desert irrigated by the Columbia and Snake rivers.
regions.styles: Burgundian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from Oregon; ripe, structured Bordeaux and Rhône reds and aromatic Riesling from Washington.
regions.classification: American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) such as Willamette Valley (with nine sub-AVAs), Southern Oregon, Columbia Gorge, Columbia Valley, Yakima Valley and Walla Walla Valley.
facts: Oregon and Washington together grow about 5% of US wine; Washington is second to California.
Walla Walla Valley is one of the few AVAs that straddle two states.
The Missoula Floods 15,000 years ago spread rich soil across the Willamette and Columbia valleys.

regions.name: Willamette Valley
regions.summary: Oregon's heart and the home of New World Pinot Noir: about 150 miles of valley south of Portland, sheltered from the Pacific by the Coast Range. Nine sub-AVAs sit inside it.
regions.climate: Cool, wet winters and dry, mild summers with long autumns. Ripening is slow, so wines keep their freshness.
regions.styles: Elegant, red-fruited Pinot Noir, crisp Pinot Gris and cool-climate Chardonnay; also traditional-method sparkling wine.
regions.history: David Lett of Eyrie Vineyards planted the first Pinot Noir here in 1965. His 1975 South Block Pinot placed in the top ten at a 1979 Paris tasting and put Oregon on the world map.
facts: Willamette is pronounced 'wil-AM-it', rhyming with 'dammit'.
Oregon's rule for a varietal label is 90% (75% for Cabernet), stricter than most of the US.
The valley sits near the 45th parallel, the same latitude as Bordeaux and Piedmont.

regions.name: Dundee Hills
regions.summary: The first and most famous sub-AVA: a ring of low hills of red, iron-rich volcanic Jory soil, home to Eyrie, Domaine Drouhin and Archery Summit.
regions.styles: Silky, perfumed Pinot Noir with red cherry and spice.

regions.name: Eola-Amity Hills
regions.summary: Hills west of Salem cooled by the Van Duzer Corridor's ocean winds: Pinot Noir with energy, structure and dark fruit.
regions.climate: Cooled by afternoon winds from the Van Duzer Gap in the Coast Range.

regions.name: Ribbon Ridge
regions.summary: The smallest AVA in Oregon (about 3,350 acres), a ridge inside Chehalem Mountains with a single marine-sediment soil, Willakenzie.
regions.styles: Concentrated, dark-fruited Pinot Noir.

regions.name: Yamhill-Carlton
regions.summary: A horseshoe of foothills on the west side of the valley, with old marine sandstone soils and Pinot Noir of spice and supple tannins.

regions.name: McMinnville
regions.summary: The foothills near the town of McMinnville, higher and cooler, on marine sediment and basalt soils.
regions.climate: Higher elevation (200 to 1,000 ft) and cool winds from the coast.

regions.name: Chehalem Mountains
regions.summary: A 20-mile ridge near Portland with three different soils (volcanic, marine and loess), so its Pinot Noir ranges from lithe to powerful.

regions.name: Van Duzer Corridor
regions.summary: Named after the gap in the Coast Range that lets the Pacific's cool afternoon breeze into the valley. Thick-skinned, intense Pinot Noir.
regions.climate: Ocean winds cool the vineyards by up to 15 F in the afternoon.

regions.name: Laurelwood District
regions.summary: The newest north-valley AVA, on the slopes of Chehalem Mountains with deep wind-blown Laurelwood loess soil.

regions.name: Tualatin Hills
regions.summary: The hills just west of Portland: wind-blown Laurelwood soils and some of the state's oldest vineyards.

regions.name: Lower Long Tom
regions.summary: A small, young AVA in the southern part of the valley, in the Coast Range foothills.

regions.name: Mount Pisgah, Polk County
regions.summary: A cool, south-facing area west of Salem in the Polk County hills.

regions.name: Southern Oregon
regions.summary: A warm, sun-drenched collection of valleys between the Coast Range and the Cascades, much more varied than the Willamette: Syrah, Tempranillo and Cabernet grow next to Pinot Noir.
regions.climate: Warm, dry and sunny, with elevation and river valleys cooling the nights.
regions.styles: Rich Syrah and Bordeaux blends, Tempranillo, Viognier and Pinot Noir from the cooler sites.

regions.name: Umpqua Valley
regions.summary: Oregon's oldest modern wine region, where Richard Sommer planted the state's first Pinot Noir at HillCrest in 1961. A cool-to-warm transition zone with the widest range of grapes in Oregon.

regions.name: Red Hill Douglas County
regions.summary: A tiny AVA of red volcanic soil near Oakland, inside the Umpqua Valley.

regions.name: Elkton Oregon
regions.summary: The Umpqua's cool western corner, 20 miles from the Pacific, on the Umpqua River.
regions.climate: Marine influence: the coolest part of Umpqua.

regions.name: Rogue Valley
regions.summary: A warmer, drier valley on the California border: Syrah, Cabernet and Tempranillo thrive, with Pinot Noir and Viognier on cooler sites.
regions.climate: Hot summers; elevation ranges from 1,000 to 2,000 ft.

regions.name: Applegate Valley
regions.summary: A scenic valley within the Rogue Valley with granite soils and cooler nights; varied reds and whites in a small-production setting.

regions.name: Columbia Gorge
regions.summary: A dramatic river gorge between Oregon and Washington where the climate flips from wet forest in the west to dry desert in the east, all in 40 miles.
regions.climate: Annual rainfall drops from 40 inches in the west to under 10 inches in the east; constant winds.

regions.name: Columbia Valley
regions.summary: Washington's giant AVA (about a third of the state, 11 million acres) covering almost all of its wine grapes. Desert-dry, irrigated by the Columbia and Snake rivers, with cool nights and long sunshine.
regions.climate: Very dry (6 to 8 inches of rain), hot summers, cold winters; irrigated.
regions.styles: Bold Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah, plus crisp Riesling and Chardonnay.
regions.history: Chateau Ste. Michelle was founded in 1967; the AVA was recognized in 1984.
facts: Washington is the second largest wine producer in the US.
Most Washington vines are grown on their own roots, as sandy desert soils and cold winters limit phylloxera.

regions.name: Yakima Valley
regions.summary: Washington's first AVA (1983) and the heart of its wine country, with the Yakima River running through sun-baked hills. Home to many of the state's oldest vineyards.

regions.name: Red Mountain
regions.summary: Washington's smallest and hottest AVA, a south-facing slope producing some of the state's most powerful Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.climate: Hot and dry: the warmest AVA in the state.

regions.name: Rattlesnake Hills
regions.summary: A band of hills north of the Yakima Valley with higher altitude and long hang-time for Syrah, Merlot and Cabernet.

regions.name: Snipes Mountain
regions.summary: A small ridge with some of Washington's oldest vines (planted in 1917) and unusual soils of sandy loam.

regions.name: Candy Mountain
regions.summary: A small, warm basalt hill beside Red Mountain, planted in the 2000s.

regions.name: Horse Heaven Hills
regions.summary: A long south-facing slope above the Columbia River: wind, sun and sandy loess give ripe, concentrated reds. Home to some of Washington's biggest vineyards.

regions.name: Wahluke Slope
regions.summary: A hot, dry, south-facing slope along the Columbia, a major source of Syrah, Merlot and Cabernet.

regions.name: Walla Walla Valley
regions.summary: A famous Bordeaux-style region straddling the Oregon-Washington border, with some wines named after one state but made from vines in both.
regions.climate: Slightly cooler and wetter than the Yakima Valley, with a longer ripening season.
regions.styles: Structured Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah.

regions.name: The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater
regions.summary: An ancient riverbed covered in cobblestones, in Oregon's portion of Walla Walla, giving powerful, savoury Syrah unlike anywhere else.

regions.name: Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley
regions.summary: A cool, high-latitude part of the Columbia Valley around the Quincy Basin, known for crisp Riesling and Chardonnay.

regions.name: Royal Slope
regions.summary: A warm slope in the north of the Columbia Valley, between the Saddle Mountains and the Frenchman Hills.

regions.name: White Bluffs
regions.summary: A tiny new AVA on the Columbia River near the Hanford Reach, with sandy loess soils.

regions.name: Goose Gap
regions.summary: A small, warm AVA west of Red Mountain.

regions.name: The Burn of Columbia Valley
regions.summary: A newer AVA on the Columbia River's Oregon side near Hermiston, known for warm days and windy, sandy soils.

regions.name: Lake Chelan
regions.summary: A cool lake-side AVA in north-central Washington, one of the northernmost wine areas on the west coast.

regions.name: Rocky Reach
regions.summary: A narrow AVA along the Columbia River north of Wenatchee.

regions.name: Naches Heights
regions.summary: A small AVA in the Yakima foothills on a flat plateau of wind-blown loess, outside the Columbia Valley.

regions.name: Puget Sound
regions.summary: The cool, wet western Washington around Seattle: lean white wines from Madeleine Angevine, Siegerrebe and Pinot Gris.
regions.climate: Marine, mild and rainy, similar to northern Germany.

regions.name: Romania
regions.summary: The fifth-largest wine producer in Europe, with 2,000 years of vines, wide hills from the Carpathians to the Black Sea and native grapes such as Fetească.
regions.climate: Temperate continental, with warm summers and cold winters; the Carpathian arc and the Black Sea shape the climate.
regions.styles: Fruity, off-dry whites and increasing quality in dry reds; Fetească Neagră is the leading red native.
regions.classification: Eight wine regions and 40+ DOCs (denumire de origine controlată), such as Cotnari, Dealu Mare and Murfatlar.
regions.history: The Greeks planted vines on the Black Sea coast in the 7th century BC; the Dacians already made wine. Cotnari was famous in medieval Moldavia as the wine of kings.
facts: Romania has the second-largest vineyard area of any EU country after France.
The Murfatlar region on the Black Sea is known for its sweet, late-harvest wines.

regions.name: Transylvania
regions.summary: The high plateau inside the Carpathians: cool, aromatic whites such as Fetească Regală and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Moldavia (Romania)
regions.summary: The largest vineyard region, on the eastern slopes of the Carpathians. It includes Cotnari (sweet, historic whites) and Vrancea, the biggest single wine county.

regions.name: Muntenia & Oltenia
regions.summary: The southern foothills: sunny slopes of Dealu Mare ('Big Hill') with Cabernet, Merlot and Fetească Neagră. Romania's top reds.
regions.climate: The warmest wine area.

regions.name: Banat & Crișana
regions.summary: The western plains next to Hungary and Serbia, with small, historic districts such as Recaș and Miniș.

regions.name: Dobrogea
regions.summary: The Black Sea coast and Danube delta: warm and dry, home of Murfatlar, famed for late-harvest sweet wines.

regions.name: Slovenia
regions.summary: A small country at the crossroads of the Alps, the Mediterranean and the Pannonian plain, with a deep wine culture, orange wines, white blends and a trio of wine regions.
regions.climate: Alpine in the north, Mediterranean on the coast and continental in the east.
regions.styles: Fresh whites from Štajerska, rich Rebula and orange wines in Goriška Brda, Teran from the Karst, and the light red-white blend Cviček.
regions.classification: Three wine regions (Podravje, Posavje, Primorska) divided into nine districts (including Štajerska Slovenija, Goriška Brda, Vipavska dolina, Kras).
facts: In Maribor, the Old Vine is the oldest vine in the world, about 400 years old and still bearing fruit.
Goriška Brda is a hill region that continues over the border into Italy's Collio, with the same ripe, skin-contact white wines.

regions.name: Podravje
regions.summary: The north-east: Slovenia's biggest region of gentle hills along the Drava and Mura rivers, famous for crisp, aromatic whites and sparkling wine.

regions.name: Štajerska Slovenija
regions.summary: Styria on the Austrian border, with steep slopes of Šipon (Furmint) and Welschriesling, Slovenia's best white wine area.

regions.name: Prekmurje
regions.summary: The flat Pannonian plain in the far north-east, bordering Hungary and Austria.

regions.name: Posavje
regions.summary: The Sava valley in the south-east, famous for Cviček, a light, high-acid red blend.

regions.name: Primorska
regions.summary: The western coastal region, with Mediterranean and Alpine influence and the most distinctive white wines of Slovenia.

regions.name: Goriška Brda
regions.summary: Rolling hills known as the Tuscany of Slovenia. Sweet-spiced white blends and skin-contact orange wines made from Rebula.

regions.name: Vipavska Dolina
regions.summary: A wind-swept valley (the Bora blows here) with local white grapes such as Zelen and Pinela.

regions.name: Kras
regions.summary: The rocky Karst plateau, with red 'terra rossa' soil that colours the Teran: a tangy, deep-purple red.

regions.name: Slovenian Istria
regions.summary: The tiny Slovenian coast with Malvazija and Refošk.

regions.name: Switzerland
regions.summary: Small, steep and mostly drunk at home: Swiss wine hardly leaves the country. Mountain terraces make crisp Chasselas, lively Pinot Noir and rare local grapes such as Petite Arvine and Cornalin.
regions.climate: Alpine to continental, with sunny, sheltered slopes by lakes and in the high Alpine valleys.
regions.styles: Light, mineral white Chasselas (Fendant), Pinot Noir and Gamay blends such as Dôle, and Merlot from Ticino.
regions.classification: Swiss AOCs follow cantons and districts: Valais, Vaud, Genève, Ticino and others, with Grand Cru in Vaud and Valais.
regions.history: The Romans planted vines on the shores of Lake Geneva; medieval monks built the terraces of Lavaux, now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
facts: Chasselas (known as Fendant in Valais) is the most planted white grape and shows the soil of each place very clearly.
Only about 2% of Swiss wine is exported.

regions.name: Valais
regions.summary: The biggest and driest wine canton, in the upper Rhône valley between high Alps. Terraced vineyards up to 1,100 m, with the most varied grapes in the country.
regions.climate: Very dry and sunny, one of the driest places in Switzerland.

regions.name: Vaud
regions.summary: North shore of Lake Geneva: Chasselas country, with the famous terraces of Lavaux, La Côte and Chablais.

regions.name: Geneva
regions.summary: A city canton ringed by vines. The third-largest wine canton, with a mild lake climate and a wide range of grapes.

regions.name: Three Lakes
regions.summary: The lakes of Neuchâtel, Biel and Murten at the foot of the Jura: light Chasselas, Pinot Noir and the pink Œil de Perdrix.

regions.name: Ticino
regions.summary: The Italian-speaking south: Merlot rules, from fresh rosé-style blanc de noirs to deeper reds, on warm slopes above the Lombard lakes.

regions.name: German-speaking Switzerland
regions.summary: The north and east: many small family vineyards. Pinot Noir (Blauburgunder) is the main grape, and Graubünden's Bündner Herrschaft makes some of the best.

regions.name: Lavaux
regions.summary: A UNESCO World Heritage site: 800 years of vine terraces rising 400 m from Lake Geneva, with Chasselas wines from Dézaley and Saint-Saphorin.

regions.name: La Côte
regions.summary: The long, gentle slope between Lausanne and Geneva: the biggest Vaud district, with light and fresh Chasselas.

regions.name: Chablais
regions.summary: The Rhône delta at the eastern end of Lake Geneva, with famous names such as Yvorne, Aigle and Bex.

regions.name: Texas & the Southwest
regions.summary: Hot, high and dry: Texas (the second most visited wine region in the US), New Mexico (America's oldest wine tradition, 1629) and Arizona grow Mediterranean grapes such as Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Viognier and Grenache.
regions.climate: Hot summers, big day-night swings at altitude, and very little rain. Cool, high plains sites and the Hill Country do best.
regions.styles: Rhône and Spanish varieties: Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Viognier, Grenache, plus Bordeaux reds and sparkling.
regions.classification: American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) such as Texas Hill Country, Texas High Plains, Mesilla Valley, Sonoita and Willcox.
facts: About 85% of Texas grapes are grown in the High Plains near Lubbock, on high, dry plateau.
New Mexico's first vines were planted by Spanish missionaries in the 1620s, the oldest wine region in the United States.

regions.name: Texas Hill Country
regions.summary: The state's best-known wine area, in the rolling hills around Austin and San Antonio. The second-largest AVA in the US by area and a big wine-tourism draw.

regions.name: Fredericksburg in the Texas Hill Country
regions.summary: A German-settled town and the Hill Country's wine hub: dozens of tasting rooms in a few miles.

regions.name: Bell Mountain
regions.summary: A small, high AVA of granite soils in the Hill Country, the first in Texas.

regions.name: Texas High Plains
regions.summary: A high, flat, windy plateau around Lubbock at over 3,000 ft. It grows most of the state's grapes, with cool nights and strong sun.

regions.name: Texoma
regions.summary: North Texas along the Red River and the Oklahoma border.

regions.name: Texas Davis Mountains
regions.summary: A remote mountain AVA in West Texas, at over 4,500 ft.

regions.name: Escondido Valley
regions.summary: A small desert valley in the far west of Texas.

regions.name: Mesilla Valley
regions.summary: South New Mexico and a corner of Texas along the Rio Grande, where Spanish friars planted vines in the 1600s.

regions.name: Middle Rio Grande Valley
regions.summary: New Mexico's central valley, with Albuquerque at the centre and sparkling wine as a speciality.

regions.name: Mimbres Valley
regions.summary: A very small, high AVA in south-west New Mexico.

regions.name: Sonoita
regions.summary: Arizona's first AVA, a high grassland valley south-east of Tucson at about 5,000 ft with cool nights.

regions.name: Willcox
regions.summary: A high desert plateau in south-east Arizona that grows most of the state's grapes.

regions.name: Verde Valley
regions.summary: A river valley near Sedona with a growing group of wineries.

regions.name: Turkey
regions.summary: One of the world's biggest grape growers (mostly for eating and raisins), and the cradle of winemaking in Anatolia, 4,000 years old. A small, fast-improving quality wine industry uses over 1,000 native grape varieties.
regions.climate: Varied: Mediterranean on the coast, continental and cold on the high central plateau and the east.
regions.styles: Dry reds, fresh mineral whites, rakı (aniseed spirit) and a growing group of boutique wineries.
regions.classification: Wine areas by region (Thrace & Marmara, Aegean, Central Anatolia, Eastern Anatolia, Mediterranean) with geographical indication (PGI) status.
regions.history: The Hittites made wine in Anatolia 4,000 years ago; Dionysus, god of wine, was worshipped in the Aegean cities of Asia Minor. Noah's ark is said to have landed on Mount Ararat in the east.
facts: Boğazkere and Öküzgözü are the two great red grapes of eastern Anatolia; they are often blended, one for tannin and the other for fruit.
In Cappadocia, vines grow among tuff fairy chimneys and cave cellars.

regions.name: Thrace & Marmara
regions.summary: The European corner of Turkey, around the Sea of Marmara: about 40% of Turkish wine, with Bordeaux grapes and the coastal Şarköy-Mürefte area.

regions.name: Aegean
regions.summary: Sunny hills and islands near İzmir (Urla, Manisa, Denizli): the biggest area for table grapes and raisins, and a growing hub for fresh, Mediterranean wines.

regions.name: Central Anatolia
regions.summary: The high plateau around Ankara and Cappadocia, with big day-night swings: Emir (Cappadocia, a crisp white), Kalecik Karası (a light, aromatic red) and Narince (Tokat).
regions.climate: Continental, with hot summers and bitterly cold winters.

regions.name: Eastern Anatolia
regions.summary: The mountains and basins of the east, near the Euphrates and Tigris: the home of Öküzgözü and Boğazkere, the country's top reds.

regions.name: Mediterranean & South
regions.summary: A hot coastal strip with a few vineyards at altitude in the Taurus mountains.

regions.name: Uruguay
regions.summary: South America's fourth wine producer, and the home of Tannat, a grape from south-west France that has become the national red. Near-ocean vines make fresh Albariño and elegant reds.
regions.climate: Maritime and humid with rain at harvest, tempered by Atlantic and River Plate breezes, closer to Bordeaux than Mendoza.
regions.styles: Tannat (deep, tannic reds with fruit and spice), Albariño (a salty, fresh white), Bordeaux blends and a growing sparkling and rosé scene.
regions.classification: The national wine regions are Montevideo, Canelones, Colonia, San José, Maldonado, Rocha and the north (Rivera, Salto, Tacuarembó, Rivera).
regions.history: Tannat came with Basque settlers in 1870, led by Pascual Harriague. Today it is Uruguay's flagship, and a lighter, fresher modern style is replacing the old tannic wines.
facts: Uruguay has about 200 wineries, mostly small family estates in the south.
Pascual Harriague's name is still used in Uruguay for Tannat ('Harriague').

regions.name: Canelones & Montevideo
regions.summary: The country's biggest wine area, on the outskirts of the capital: about 60% of production. Cool, humid weather and clay soils.

regions.name: Colonia
regions.summary: Along the River Plate in the west, with historic Colonia del Sacramento and some old family estates. Warmer than Canelones.

regions.name: Maldonado & Rocha
regions.summary: The Atlantic coast near Punta del Este and the Garzón area: sea breezes and granite hills give the freshest wines in the country, led by Albariño and Tannat.

regions.name: Northern Uruguay
regions.summary: A warmer, inland area on the border with Brazil and Argentina, with sandstone and basalt soils.

soils.serra-gaucha: Basalt and clay at 600 to 800 m.
soils.niagara-peninsula: Clay, limestone and glacial silt on gentle benches.
soils.istria-kvarner: Red clay (terra rossa) over limestone, and grey marl.
soils.sussex: South Downs chalk, greensand and clay.
soils.kakheti: Alluvial gravel and clay on the valley floor, limestone and clay on the slopes.
soils.kartli: Brown and limestone soils on the hills along the Kura River.
soils.monticello: Red clay and granite on the Blue Ridge foothills.
soils.snake-river-valley: Ancient lake sediment and volcanic ash.
soils.finger-lakes: Glacial shale, slate and limestone on steep lakeside slopes.
soils.long-island: Sandy loam over glacial gravel, which drains well.
soils.willamette-valley: Three main soils: ancient volcanic Jory (Dundee Hills), marine sediment (Yamhill-Carlton, Eola-Amity) and wind-blown loess (Chehalem, Ribbon Ridge).
soils.dundee-hills: Red Jory soil: deep volcanic basalt clay, rich in iron.
soils.yamhill-carlton: Sandy, marine sedimentary soils drained by the Coast Range.
soils.umpqua-valley: Over 150 soil types in one valley, from marine sediment to volcanic.
soils.columbia-valley-ava: Wind-blown loess, ancient flood sediment from the Missoula Floods, and basalt.
soils.red-mountain: Sandy, gravelly, low-fertility soils, with a lot of calcium carbonate.
soils.rocks-district: Basalt cobblestones left by the Walla Walla River: like Châteauneuf-du-Pape's galets.
soils.texas-high-plains: Sandy loam over limestone and caliche.
